analysis.one_liner: Paused EPA's copper limits in drinking water until federal health studies were finished.
analysis.headline: With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill died in the Senate Environment Committee without a vote, leaving EPA's copper drinking water rules in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the EPA from enforcing its national drinking water limits on copper until six months after two Centers for Disease Control studies, in Nebraska and Delaware, were finished, published in a peer-reviewed journal, and reviewed. Sen. Chuck Hagel introduced it in late July 1998, near the end of the congressional session, and the Senate environment committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Water systems — especially small systems in Nebraska and Delaware — that exceeded EPA's copper limit and would otherwise have to install treatment to reduce copper leaching into tap water. The bill would have given them at least several years of relief: the prohibition ran until six months after the CDC studies were completed, published, and reviewed. Because the text barred implementation of the copper rules generally, systems in every state would have gotten the same pause.

how_it_helps.text: Gave water systems a multi-year exemption from EPA's copper treatment requirements: the ban on implementing the rules would not lift until six months after the CDC studies in Nebraska and Delaware were completed, published in a peer-reviewed journal, and reviewed by the EPA Administrator and Nebraska.

Relieved water systems of the immediate costs of complying with the Safe Drinking Water Act's copper regulation, which requires systems exceeding EPA's action level to treat their water to keep copper from leaching into household taps.

analysis.who_pays: People drinking water that exceeds EPA's copper limit during the delay. Copper at high levels causes stomach illness, and children are the most sensitive. The prohibition covered the national copper rules, not just Nebraska's and Delaware's, so every community's copper enforcement would have paused — with no interim protection written in for anyone.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households drinking water above the copper limit

drawbacks.text: The bill would have paused copper enforcement nationwide, not just in the two states where the CDC studies were happening, since it barred implementing the national copper rules outright — leaving communities everywhere without the standard while the research ran.

The delay came with no interim protection: people served by systems above EPA's copper limit would have kept drinking that water during the studies, even though the EPA had already set the limit based on health risk, particularly stomach illness in children.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that waiting for peer-reviewed science was the bill's whole argument — the CDC studies offered a legitimate check on the rule's health basis — but the bill set no deadline for the studies, so the pause could have stretched on indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a nationwide pause in drinking water enforcement for the promise of better science. Water systems facing treatment costs would have gained real relief, but the cost fell on the people drinking the water: the copper limits would have gone unenforced everywhere until studies with no deadline were finished and reviewed, and the bill offered no interim safeguard for households above the limit. A narrower bill — tied only to the systems in the study states, with a firm end date — would have been a much more defensible ask.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last months of the session, referred to the Senate environment committee, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Hagel introduced the bill on July 31, 1998, in the final stretch of the 105th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — the standard first step — and it attracted no cosponsors.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote. The bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and nothing in it became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public is better off that the bill died: EPA's copper drinking water rules stayed in force, so the health standard the bill would have paused never lapsed. Water systems got no relief from compliance costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tap-water drinkers; the EPA rules survived

for.name: Chuck Hagel
for.role: U.S. Senator from Nebraska; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block EPA copper rule implementation pending the CDC studies; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: John Chafee
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral and took no action — no markup or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: Systems exceeding EPA's copper action level would have avoided, for years, the cost of corrosion-control treatment under the Safe Drinking Water Act. Their gain came by leaving copper limits unenforced in the taps their customers drink from, with the health risk shifted onto those customers.

The bill would have stripped the agency of its authority to implement the copper drinking water rules nationwide until the studies concluded. The delay would have undercut a public health standard the agency had issued to protect drinking water.
